title: Welcome to the Kipuka!
text: I am glad you are here and want to play by the rules. We have put a lot of time into organizing our rules to make viewing pleasurable on a variety of devices and still look good on paper. Warnings before play:Kipukas uses many small game pieces to keep track of play. All pieces should be treated as CHOKING HAZARDS and the game content is for people 13+ years of age. Do not let children under or pets play with the pieces. At all times, it is the responsibility of the legal guardians to keep all pieces out of reach of children and pets. The included chat bot (Kippa) is an alpha feature to assist players in learning the rules. Kippa can hallucinate — the rules text is always the canonical source. Interactions may be anonymously logged for debugging and improvement; no personal or identifying data is ever collected. For the full list of limitations see Using the Binder in the About Kipukas articles page in the binder. By continuing to play with our products, you acknowledge that Kipukas accepts no liability for damages incurred by the misuse of our products.

title: Game Forward (You may skip if you prefer)
text: Kipukas is a game which draws the best concepts from creature card games and melds them with land conquering play. While I have personally enjoyed playing in other competitive card based games, I grew frustrated with becoming attached to certain characters, styles, and strategies only to have them become re-released, competitively invalidated by the latest deck release, or banned due to corporate oversight. On top of this, game companies tend to produce very poor quality cards which are not meant to last, yet some manage to reach unfathomable prices not worthy of the underlying paper. Kipukas seeks to be different. I want Kipukas, both as a game and a durable good, to outlast myself. By making cards which are updatable without new releases, we keep all the cards we produce competitively relevant. Additionally, with most cards produced at low rates, Kipukas challengers are much more diverse. The durability of our cards as game pieces are protected by the fact that we can update a broken card mechanic POST SALE. This protects your value from being wasted due to our short sightedness or oversight. While most land conquering games are enjoyable as well as strategically challenging, I was dissatisfied with the amount of pure luck the games hinge on. By combining with the complex card v. card mechanics, Kipukas battles feel more engaging, all the while retaining the larger scale strategies of the land conquering play. While complex and entertaining play is great, I want Kipukas to take on deep meaning and help spread it to many wonderful people in this world. Kipukas will set industry standards for innovative play, company interaction, and support of all who make Kipukas awesome. Lastly, I hope many find Kipukas as enjoyable as I have found my competition. Better yet, more so.

title: Background (You may skip if you prefer)
text: Kipukas is a visualization of a world where society creates new worlds as they see fit. Each of these worlds are known as kipuka, which comes from the Hawaiian word for 'land between lava flows', and is symbolic of the destruction and rebirth of worlds. Cloning and genetic manipulation are the preferred methods of populating, expanding, and manipulating the worlds. In the game, the kipukas are represented by the 3D game map and the souls take life in the cards. The game represents the strife to control the world, while the players provide the motivation for the strife. The companion book series, Conscious Territory, which takes a deep dive into these concepts, is in progress with the first three chapters released and ready for reading. I have personally enjoyed working the concepts and hope you will enjoy contemplating them as well.

title: Winning the game
text: Get off to a good start and establish base camps across the board. Win fights and think strategically to take your frenemies base camps and if you dare their capital! Once one player claims all base camps and capitals, they dominate the kipuka and win the game. See Capitals and Base Camps.

title: Pieces
text: Kipukas relies on oversized cards, 3d printed game pieces and game boards, and a mat for play organization. We currently make all of these as a batch process in-house. The cards we produce do not include the play mechanics on the card as, to my knowledge, all other card companies do. Instead, we let the artist’s work be as big and beautiful as possible. In fact, we do not even let the name of the card get in the way of showcasing artistic talent. Instead, we have made the play data for every card we produce accessible from the QR code printed on each card's back. Technically, this means the back of every kipukas card is wholly unique and identifiable. However, unless you can scan a QR code with your eye it probably won’t help you much. Additionally, the card art on the back helps camouflage the QR from cameras at a distance making remote cheating quite difficult to say the least.

title: Game Terminology
text:
A turn in Kipukas refers to a single day, night or storm (diel cycle) roll. Turns are shared between the players.
When a card counts time, it counts rolls. A turn and a diel cycle are the same count: every roll, whatever it shows. A day is a turn that comes up day, a night is one that comes up night, and a storm is one that comes up storm. So "the next 3 days" is the next three turns that come up day, however many nights and storms fall between them.
An action refers to enacting a play rule. You can take as many actions (playing cards, moving souls, etc.) as possible during a diel cycle, but this consists of only one turn.
A player with initiative takes the first action in a turn. Once an action is taken, the next player takes an action. This passes back and forth until either player takes initiative for the next turn.
Characters and Species are collectively called souls. While they have subtle play differences, when the term soul is used they play in the same manner for that context.
Kipuka (singular) refers to the 3D terrain that the game is played on.

title: Game Setup
text:
Place the 3D map on the outlined square printed on the mat. Gather and place the required game pieces next to both players.
Unlock your device, turn off screen sleep (using a caffeine mode app is recommended), then visit kipukas.cards (ideally on a chromium based browser). Also, it is best if your device has a fully functioning front facing "Selfie" Camera
Each player declares an affinity for one adaptation for use for the entire game. Say "My affinity is with the blank." where blank is an adaptation. For example, "My affinity is with the brutal." See Affinity. (For the list of adaptations, see The Adaptive Codex)
Determine who places their capital first. Players should each roll a D6. The player with the higher roll will place their capital first. In trade, the player with the lower roll will receive initiative for the first in-game turn. Alternatively, upon agreement between both parties, players may decide who takes which starting advantage.
One player takes the first territory by placing their capital, the other player then takes a territory with their capital. After this, each player makes claims with base camps until both players have 3 territories. This will leave 2 to 6 territories unclaimed, depending on the map in use.
Place the personal effect card that you will be using in front of you. You are not obligated to reveal what it does until you use it. If you do not have a personal effect card, use the default effect. See Personal Effects Note: Starter Decks do not include personal effect cards
Respectfully shuffle each other’s decks, then hand the deck back to its owner. DON’T BRIDGE THE CARDS! Slide the cards along one another, lifting then placing small groups to change the card order. Remember that these cards are fine art and should be respected as such!
Draw three cards from the top of the deckNOTE: This is your absolute max hand size. You cannot have more than three cards in your hand at any given time. Also, you cannot play more than 3 cards from your hand within a diel roll
Begin the game on the turn of the player who placed their capital second. The first diel cycle is always day, followed by night, followed by day. In this way, both players get the chance to play cards, refresh their hand and move once before diel cycle rolling starts.

title: Diel Cycle and Turn Advancement
text: If you followed along up to this point, you should now be ready to play the game! Let’s go! The first 3 turns are predetermined to always be day, then night, then day to jump start the game. After these, the first thing the players need to do before every turn is roll the diel die. It has faces that show a sun (day), a moon (night), and lighting/wind (storm). This roll dictates the actions you can take over the course of this turn, as is detailed further in this section. If present, the numbers indicate the order actions are taken.   While it may seem counter intuitive for night not to follow day, don't think of the diel cycle die a being directly attached to hours of a day. Rather think of the roll as dictating the productivity of that day.   Each diel roll, and its actions, apply to all players for that turn.

title: Day Actions (Blazing Sun)
text:
The turn starts with the player holding initiative.

You may take initiative right off the bat, even with enemies in your territory. Remember, you forego your turn of attack and your ability to take any more actions for this day by taking initiative. Be prepared for whatever actions your opponent might take against you!

Otherwise, if enemies are in your territory, choose to attack or retreat. See Attack, Defense, Retreat, and Healing as well as Maps (The Kipukas): Claiming Territories: Contention

Once you have dealt with contention carried over from the previous day the active player has four options:The active player may place one card into play. Cards available for play during day are terrain features, traps, and souls in revealed or unrevealed position on a territory you control. See Card Variations.ORThe active player reveals anor moves 1 soul to adjacent stands within their movement range. See Maps (The Kipukas): Movement

Upon movement into a territory where your opponent has unrevealed cards, your opponent will have you roll a D20 for trap activation/detection. If one of these cards becomes activated, deal with the consequences. See Card Activation Sequence and Trap Cards.
If the movement or territory stand that you moved onto is occupied, then attack the soul(s) on that stand. See Attack, Defense, Retreat, and Healing
If the stand occupied is a territory stand, and it is not under contention, place or replace a base camp token on the territory. See Maps (The Kipukas): Claiming Territories.

ORThe active player uses their personal effect. See Personal Effect Cards.ORThe active player heals with one of their healers. See Healing.

After any new contention is resolved (i.e. keal means bout was won or put on pause due to loss) play moves to the other player. Now they resolve any existing conflicts (choosing to fight or retreat), then optionally take one of the options of step 4 (play a card, move a soul, use their personal effect or heal) and resolve any resulting contention.

Steps 2-5 repeat until one player decides they have no moves left. At this point they can take initiative unless it has already been claimed. At this point the other player may repeat steps 3-5 as many times as they desire.

Once both players have exhausted the moves they want to make, either player may roll for the next diel cycle.

title: Night Actions (Crescent Moon)
text:
Like during the day, the player holding initiative begins the turn. The active player can take one of the following actions before the other player takes an action. Each player may only perform each action once per night, but can choose the order the actions are taken 
If you so desire, you can move your hand to the bottom of the deck. (Do not refill your hand this action)
You may draw cards to fill your hand back to 3 cards if your hand is diminished.
You may choose to craft any items, then play or hide them. See Item Cards: Crafting.
You may play a sabotage card. See Sabotage cards.
You may activate your personal effect. See Personal Effect Cards.
You may heal with one of your healers. See Healing.
You may call initiative for the next diel cycle (No further actions can be taken this turn)
 Once both players have exhausted the moves they want to make, either player may roll for the next diel cycle.

title: Storm Actions (Lightning / Wind)
text:
Take Shelter! If a storm is rolled, any card caught in it (not within a capital or base camp) will take KEAL means damage and any downed cards will be wasted. See KEAL Means Damage, Healing, and Tolerance. Some habitats change the damage a storm does; see Habitat Effects.   Note:   
Storm rolls apply to both players at the same time.Initiative does not apply to storm rolls. It carries over from the previous day/night to the next day/night.Once both players have applied damage to all applicable souls, either player may roll for the next diel cycle.

When souls move onto a movement or territory stand in a territory controlled by their opponent a series of events might occur. If your opponent has any unrevealed cards you must roll a D20 for activation and detection. See Trap Cards. The order in which card effects are applied follows:

title: Character and Species (Collectively Soul) Cards
text: These cards are the soul of Kipukas. Species cards tell the story of a species as a whole, while characters tell the story of an individual within a species. The one playable difference between the two is tameability: a species must be tamed to be under your control, while a character needs no taming. Throughout this guide, we refer to these as souls or soul cards when the context applies to both characters and species. Most souls have the ability to move and interact with traps and items, unless otherwise stated. Each soul has a core adaptation and 1 or more KEAL means made up of adaptations. Additionally, each soul specifies how many movement/territory stands it can traverse in a day (Movement Range), hearts that track the injuries to its KEAL means and its Final Blow (Combat), additional play rules (Game Effects), which dice it rolls for attack and defense (Combat Die Rolls), preferred territory type (Habitat), and a tie breaking sequence (Brawl Power).   We encourage you to develop story lines for your favorite cards to make the game more imaginative and personal. These should be pliable details developed through situational game play in order to form the soul's personality. Additionally, if some detail of game strategy, like increasing the power of a dragon with a stick, seems janky, you can call out the move as ridiculous even if the move is otherwise valid. If you learn by example better than explanation, read the Contention Resolution Example in Attack, Defense, Retreat and Healing first then reference this section as needed. As interest grows, I plan on publishing play-through videos to kipukas.cards.

title: KEAL Means
text: Each card has a unique set of qualities used in attack and defense called KEAL means. These must be injured or broken to defeat the card. See Attack, Defense, Retreat, and Healing. Each part is composed of a material with adaptations of its own. By the way, KEAL stands for Keep Everyone ALive and emphasizes the importance of every card you play.

title: Materials
text: KEAL means represent some physical trait or object that helps represent the soul it belongs to. These are all made of some manner of matter or energy, and can be thought of as materials. These materials share the same adaptations presented by The Adaptive Codex which are also used for the card's core adaptation. The major difference between these qualities is that a core adaptation represents the soul's general adaptation, where KEAL means detail the card's individual preferences/traits. Where each card only has one core adaptation, each KEAL means may be represented by 3 adaptations. These bonuses stack and counteract each other, where each adaptation of the attacking KEAL means interacts with each adaptation of the defending KEAL means. Use the fists tool in the tool bar on kipukas.cards to determine the roll modifier between KEAL means for a given attack.

title: Habitat
text: Whether by God or by man, this is where the soul was created to live. Habitat shapes how a soul gets across the kipuka: how it moves through a territory, crosses water, and weathers storms. Each territory's geography brings the effects of its habitat, listed below. Card effects may also target souls by habitat. Habitat does not modify battle rolls: KEAL means bouts and the Final Blow are fought the same in any territory.

title: Habitat Effects
text:
Mountain 
Primary Effect: Mountaineers are not fazed by thin air, steep slopes or loose rock and move normally.
Secondary Effect: Other souls have one less stand of Movement Range on any day they enter or cross a mountain territory.
 Forest 
Primary Effect: Foresters skillfully read the terrain, navigate the canopy, and track wildlife to cross safely.
Secondary Effect: Other souls get lost. While in a forest territory they move as a rogue does: number the paths from their stand 1-6 and roll a D6 for each step.
 Plains 
Primary Effect: Plains dwellers know the only safe shelter is a sturdy one and take no storm damage in the plains.
Secondary Effect: Other souls receive 2 storm damage instead of 1 in the plains.
 Water 
Primary Effect: Aquatic dwellers move in water without boats or rolling to swim  
Secondary Effect: Other souls either need to ride a boat or swim to cross. Boats are crafted. Souls swim by rolling 2+2: a 2 on each of two D6. 🐟
 Volcanic Ground 
Primary Effect: Volcanic dwellers are immune to volcanic area damage  
Secondary Effect: Other souls take volcanic area damage: 1 KEAL means once per diel cycle while in a volcanic ground territory
 Underground 
Primary Effect: Underground dwellers can travel through underground tunnels  
Secondary Effect: Underground dwellers can make underground tunnels
 Digital Cloud 
Primary Effect: Occupy no space in territory: they do not count toward the 3 souls per player a territory can host  
Secondary Effect: Are unable to take or hold base camps or capitals
 Heavens 
Primary Effect: Heavens dwellers fly over territory without interacting with the cards in the territory below during movement. This does not apply to the territory they land in.
 Nomad 
Primary Effect: Nomads understand many environments, read the weather and know when to shelter. They take one less storm damage: none from an ordinary storm, and 1 in the plains.

text: This is the predominate structure of the soul. After inflicting the necessary number of injuries on the card, you must best the card in a crushing final attack. This pits the inner-self of each soul against one another. Each soul possesses a core adaptation and a motivation which effects the roll of a Final Blow attack. Group effects, from a personal effect for example, might be applied based on the soul.

title: Tameability
text:
α mechanic that applies only to species cards. Some species are easy to work with while others are quite persnickety. The tameability scale represents this phenomenon. 0 means the species does not require taming, those with 10 are the most difficult to tame, and ∞ means the species is untameable (no amount of bonuses will tame them). Characters never need taming. A species is tame once what you bring to it stacks equally with its tameability. At this point, the soul will be under the full control of the player. Three things stack, and together they come to 10 at most: 


What you bring
Worth
Where it comes from



Affinity
3
You declared the species' adaptation as your affinity at the start of the game. All or nothing.


Card effects
up to 3
Other souls and equipment played in order to wrangle the species. These come and go during the game.


Loyalty
up to 4
Your history with that card, which is the only part that carries from one game to the next. See Loyalty.

 If the player chooses to play the creature untamed or the opponent reduces your control of the creature below its tameability then the creature becomes under its own influence, rogue. To bring it back under control, see Taming Rogue Species. Additionally, some cards will specify an ability to be played at a lower tameability rating without going rogue. In exchange, certain KEAL means or play effects will be unavailable. These can be made available by staking effects equal to the tameability after the species enters play. Two things follow from the numbers. A player with no history with a card can bring 6 at most, so the hardest species answer only to those who have put in the days. And a species outside your declared affinity can be brought 7 at most, so the very hardest can only be controlled in a game where their adaptation is your affinity. 
Each species' page on kipukas.cards says whether it is under your control or rogue, and shows what your stack is made of. See Using the Binder in the About Kipukas articles page in the binder for details on the web app feature.

title: Rogue Species
text: Each day, before either player's turn, you must roll for the rogue species' movement. Assign the paths connected to its current movement/territory stand, numbers 1-6. Roll a D6, then move the species along the appropriate path. Repeat until it has moved its entire Movement Range. Movement is the responsibility of the person who originally played the rogue. If the territory it moves into is occupied by souls you or your frenemy controls, it must attack all souls (for both players) in the territory until it loses once. Rogues can move into and attack souls within either player's capital.   Players engage in contention actions (attack, retreat, or reinforce) against rogues like they do against their opponent. You can also enter an agreement with your opponent to attack rogues in a certain order anor abstain from attacking each other until the rogue is defeated. Trading or gifting cards in hand is acceptable for these negotiations (Your hand cannot have more than 3 cards, no exceptions!) Dishonesty in these agreements is entirely possible, so be careful. Souls on the top of the card stack will be attacked first.   If a rogue defeats all soul cards in a territory's base camp, remove the claim token on the territory. Rogue species must roll against trap and terrain feature cards when applicable, then reap consequences as well as benefits. Rogues must be revealed. Failure to do so will result in an immediate victory for the opposite player. If a rogue manages to defeat a player by defeating all souls in their capital while they control no base camps, the other player must defeat or tame the rogue soul. Failure to do so will result in a dual defeat.

title: Taming Rogue Species
text:
Either player can attempt to tame a rogue soul and bring it under their control. This will require the taming player's own stack for that species (their affinity, their card effects in play and their loyalty with that card) to equal its tameability. This is the same manner that species which require taming are placed normally. Taming will occur at the beginning of the day before contention is resolved. It is first available to the player with initiative. The player who attempts taming must have a fully controlled soul already in the same territory as the rogue soul. 
When your opponent tames a soul you played, hand the card to them on kipukas.cards so that its injuries go with it. See Using the Binder in the About Kipukas articles page in the binder.

title: Imprisoned Souls
text: In certain circumstances, i.e. loitering (more than 1 day) in your opponent's capital, being left unrevealed in a base camp that is taken (see Unrevealed Souls in a Fight), and under the effect of certain cards, souls can be taken prisoner. In this state the soul resides in the basecamp/capital in the territory where the prison is located and is unable to be played by the card's owner. Territories can support a max of 3 prisoners. This is in addition to the 3 souls per player normally supported. It will remain in the imprisoned state until it is liberated by meeting the conditions listed on the prison play effect or (if unspecified) the basecamp/capital is taken from the opponent. And yes, that means your loitering soul will likely be imprisoned in the capital for the entire game. However, some cards will have play mechanics that allow for imprisoned souls to be sprung. See also Capitals and Base Camps.

title: Affinity and Loyalty
text:
α feature — playable but rough, subject to refinement. Affinity is a choice you make for one game. Loyalty is the history you build with a card over many. Both are tracked on kipukas.cards, though the feature is still in early development and may change. Affinity: At the start of a game you declare an affinity for one adaptation, and it stands for the whole game. It is the same for every player, however long they have played: affinity does not grow. When a soul card's adaptation matches your declared affinity: 
you receive a +3 bonus to attack and defense rolls made for that card, Final Blow included;
if the card is a species, your affinity is worth 3 towards taming it.
 Loyalty: Each time you play a specific Character or Species card in combat, your loyalty with that card grows (once per day per card). It is worth up to 4 towards taming a species, a point at a time as your days with that card add up. How many days that takes differs from card to card, and the card does not say. Loyalty is yours and not the card's: a soul your opponent hands you answers to your own history with it, not to theirs. In time, loyalty may also grow once per match at tournaments, and a soul you came to own through an incubation card may come with loyalty already earned. Tameability interaction: When affinity, card effects, and loyalty stack equally with the species card's tameability, the card will be tamed. See Tameability for the full rules on taming and rogue species. For details on using the affinity, loyalty, and tameability tools on kipukas.cards see Using the Binder in the About Kipukas articles page in the binder.

title: Defeating a Soul (combat lifecycle)
text: In order to defeat a soul, you must first weaken them by injuring or breaking their KEAL means. This is accomplished by attacking with your soul’s KEAL means. Each soul has a certain KEAL means tolerance that it can take before becoming vulnerable to a Final Blow. Modifiers are applied based on the KEAL means being used. See Character and Species (Soul): KEAL Means. After an unsuccessful blow, the player loses their ability to attack with that card for this diel cycle. On the defender's next turn, they must choose to attack or retreat. If an effect says souls take X damage, then the damage will apply to either the KEAL means or the Final Blow. If it applies to the Final Blow, the card becomes wasted and is discarded without a Final Blow.

title: KEAL Means Damage, Healing, and Tolerance
text: As souls accrue injuries (lose KEAL means), their tolerance for new injuries becomes smaller. Injuries usually occur one at a time. See below for an example. Some can even defeat souls without contest under the correct conditions. Each KEAL means represents both a means of attack and defense as well as health. If a KEAL means become injured, it is no longer available for combat unless healed. Injuries should be marked by tapping a heart of the KEAL means in the Combat section of the card's page in the card binder, kipukas.cards. Once all KEAL means are marked as injured, the Final Blows section will appear indicating that the card is downed. This means they can't take any more punishment and become vulnerable to being engaged in a final attack. If the card either survives a Final Blow or is not engaged in a final attack, it won't be able to engage in attacks. As well, its movement speed is halved (rounding down) until it is healed. See Maps (The Kipuka): Movement: Moving Downed Souls. If a soul is caught exposed during a storm they will lose one KEAL means or if they are downed they will be wasted (if so tap the Wasted heart).   Healing has a section of its own: see Healing. Track injuries in the Combat section of each card's page on kipukas.cards. After your game, use the reset option in the toolbar to clear all KEAL state. For screenshots and details see Using the Binder in the About Kipukas articles page in the binder.

title: Healing
text:
Souls can be healed by other souls, terrain features, or items with a healing ability. The soul must be within the same territory as the healing entity or within its specified healing range. Healers can only heal a certain number of KEAL means within a certain number of diel cycles. Most healers have the ability to heal themselves under the same conditions mentioned above, unless they are downed. 
When: healing is done on your own turn, as your option at step 4 of Day Actions or as one of your Night Actions.
Where: healing is limited to cards in territories not under contention, unless the game effect states otherwise.

title: Methods of Attack Against KEAL Means
text:
The default will be dice based attacking. The attacking die (dice) will be determined by the attacking card. Affinity and materials bonuses may apply. Check the typing tools and guides for applicable bonuses.
Some cards will support mini-games where appropriate, i.e. a thief themed card may involve a timed lock picking competition.

title: Methods of Defense Against KEAL Means
text:
The default will be dice based defending. The defending die type will be determined by the defending card. Affinity and materials bonuses may apply. Check the typing guides for applicable bonuses.
When defending against mini-games there are a few options
Beat them at their own game
Attack them before they can attack you
Engage them with terrain features, traps, and items to defeat them without playing the mini-game

title: Final Blow
text: Once a soul’s KEAL means count is maxed, it may be engaged in a final attack. This must be won in order to waste the soul under attack. This attack uses the same dice as the cards use for KEAL means, but compares the cards' core adaptations rather than a chosen KEAL means. If a card does not attack, it cannot be the attacker in a Final Blow, only a defender. Additionally, each cards' fundamental motivation may help them conquer or live to see a new day. If the attack is lost, then the attack against the downed soul comes to a close. If the attack is won, the defender is wasted. See Discarding Cards and Deck Runout.

title: Brawl in the Event of a Tie
text:
If an attack results in a tie (the values of the attack and defense dice rolls, after modifiers are applied, are equal) or the mini-game does not result in a clear winner, the souls will engage in a brawl. In order to complete a brawl, both players need to look at their soul's 4 digit brawl sequence. The brawl sequence consists of letters, numbers, dashes, and underscores. In order to determine the victor, players compare the characters from left to right according to the table below. Compare the first character of each sequence. If they are the same, move to the next, and so on: the first place where the two sequences differ decides the brawl, and the stronger character there wins. From strongest to weakest the characters run A to Z, then a to z, then 9 down to 0, then the dash, then the underscore. Among letters the earlier letter in the alphabet is the stronger (B beats F); among numbers the larger is the stronger (9 beats 3). The kind of character comes first: any capital letter beats any lowercase letter (M beats m, and Z beats a), any lowercase letter beats any number, and any number beats the dash and the underscore. title: Retreat and Reinforce
text: If you are in a badly losing fight, retreating might prove beneficial. It can allow you to regroup and redeploy to a more favorable position while minimizing loss. Players may retreat souls individually or as a group to a movement/territory stand(s) after their opponent's attack fails or is stopped or after a soul is wasted, but before launching a counterattack of their own. The counterattack belongs to the player who did not just attack: their options are to counterattack, or to retreat to attempt to relieve the contention.   The stand must be within the max Movement Range of the slowest card in the group. For example, if you are retreating 2 cards in a group, one with a Movement Range of 3 and the other with a Movement Range of 1, you can only retreat both cards to a distance of 1 away for a group retreat. Once you declare a retreat, the opposing player decides if they let you go, or they challenge the escape. If the opposing player wishes to prevent the escape, the retreating player rolls 2 D6 against the opposing player's D20, and must win the roll for the retreating party to get away. If retreating souls individually, you roll for the success of each retreat in the same manner. Also, your opponent might challenge any number of retreats they wish or let some souls go without challenging the retreat.   If successful, move your party to the stand of your choosing, within the range given above. Partial retreats are allowed. Downed souls may only retreat under escort of a soul with 1 or more KEAL means. For the retreat, they move at the max movement of the escort. Afterwards, they move at the speed of the downed soul. See Moving Downed Souls. If unsuccessful, the retreating soul(s) forgo their ability to attack for the day. Additionally, if the situation is looking grim, but you don't want to lose the fight you can move souls into the conflict. This can occur in two ways. The first requires moving souls from nearby uncontended territory. This occurs with the same timing as a retreat (after an attack fails, soul is wasted, or the opponent stops attacking, but before your own counterattack) except that they are allowed to join the mess without rolling to enter. Additionally, if two territories are under contention near one another you can retreat a soul or group from one conflict to another by executing a successful retreat roll then moving the soul or party of souls into the other contended area.

title: Card Game Effects
text:
Every card says how it changes play in its Game Effects. A few things hold for all of them: 
The card comes first. A card effect supersedes the standing rules it contradicts. Where the card is silent, the standing rules apply.
Timing. Each class of card has its usual time of use, given in its own section of these rules. If an effect is used at another time, as a situational or an instant effect is, its card says so explicitly.
A soul named by an adaptation. Unless stated otherwise, "a Mechanical soul" means a soul whose core adaptation is Mechanical, and so on for the other adaptations. The adaptations of its KEAL means do not count.
Rolls. An effect that modifies a soul's rolls without saying which applies to the rolls that look for a threshold, not a pattern. Battle rolls and retreat rolls: yes. The roll to swim and the trap roll: no.
Constantly downed. Unless its card modifies the condition explicitly, a soul that is constantly downed suffers everything a downed soul does but the movement and attack restrictions. A storm that catches it exposed wastes it, for one, and an effect that targets downed souls targets it. It can still only be engaged in a Final Blow once every one of its KEAL means is injured.
Area effects. An effect on all souls on a stand or in a territory reaches the unrevealed souls and the prisoners there too.

 Combat Setup# In the above examples, we have our character, Hilbert, locked in battle with a species card called the Myrthvither Raven. The defending card's (Hilbert's) adaptation matches the player's declared affinity, so the card receives a bonus of 3 to all rolls made by the card. The first attack launched will be a KEAL means attack. The battle is taking place in a forest, which is Hilbert's habitat, but habitat does not change battle rolls: it matters for how souls move through the territory and weather its storms. Next, each player chooses a KEAL means. With the fists tool in multiplayer mode, each player submits their choice on their own device and the tool reveals both at the same time. Without it, each player writes their choice down (a mini dry erase board is handy for this) and, on the count of three, players reveal their choice to one another at the same time. These will be the keal means used for the remainder of this combat. Defense# Hilbert will use his King's Mojo (his only choice) to defend against the Raven's Symbiont Barrage. Each KEAL means is chosen by the card's owner, and lasts for all combat between these souls on this day. The bonus will need to be determined using the fists tool on kipukas.cards anor using the provided typing table guide if you prefer an arduous manual check. A key thing to note is that each type has a different effect on the other type's attack power. This adds or subtracts up to three points from the roll PER TYPE INTERACTION. This can really influence the result of the bout. As an extreme example, if a Cenozoic-Decrepit-Angelic KEAL means attacks a Decrepit-Angelic-Brutal KEAL means it will receive a crushing -13 to its roll. If it only rolls 2 D6 (quite common for cards with effects) it is an instant loss. However, in Hilbert's case the attack die modifier decreases the raven's attack roll by 6 (decrepit to angelic -1, decrepit to avian -2, decrepit to energetic +1, arboreal to angelic +2, arboreal to avian -3, arboreal to energetic -3 summed together equal -6). If the attack wins (which it has a miserable chance of accomplishing), the defender’s (Hilbert's) KEAL means becomes injured and the attacker has the opportunity to push on and attack again. This continues until the attacker loses, chooses to stop the attack, or the defender's last KEAL means becomes injured. Hilbert rolls with 2 D6 dice whereas the Myrthvither Raven rolls no dice at all: its Base 3 gives it a 3 in place of a roll. See What Modifies a Roll?. This coupled with the type advantage of Hilbert's KEAL means ensures his victory in this defense. So, the turn ends for the attacker. For the Myrthvither Raven it would end worse than that. By its card it is wasted the moment it loses a KEAL means bout, attacking or defending, and it has just lost one. This is where its player's personal effect comes in. Suspended Animation is used at that very moment: the raven is suspended instead of wasted. It cannot be wasted this turn, but it cannot move and cannot attack this turn either. Retreat, Reinforce, or Counter Attack# Now Hilbert has several options. If he is worried about the raven receiving reinforcements he can opt to retreat by winning a dice throw. Additionally, as long as Hilbert has friendly souls nearby they join in on the fun and reinforce Hilbert's attack. See Retreat and Reinforcement. However, Hilbert is feeling his kingly confidence and thinking about all the loving he will receive as a war hero. He is going to attack the Myrthvither Raven alone. Normally, this would involve the reverse role of the previous scenario, but the Myrthvither Raven is special. It modifies how the opponent can engage it at the expense of having no tolerance for KEAL means injury. It is constantly downed, and the first time it loses a KEAL means bout it is wasted without going to a Final Blow. In order to face the Myrthvither, Hilbert must successfully roll the standard detection (a 17, 18, 19, or 20 on a D20) to find the raven. Assuming this is successful the raven will likely be defeated due to being weak compared to the almighty King Hilbert. The raven is a mere scout in the presence of greatness after all. Hilbert's King's Mojo strikes the Symbiont Barrage, the KEAL means the raven chose for this combat, and wins: the Symbiont Barrage is injured, and its heart is tapped. A lost bout would waste the raven all over again, but today it is suspended: it cannot be wasted this turn. So the current territory will remain under contention, and the fighting will resume the next day with the player who claims initiative attacking first. Alternatively, either Hilbert or the raven can be attacked by a reinforcing soul moved into the territory during this day. Clutching Victory# The fighting should resume the next day. Hilbert, however, is a king, and a king has thralls: he spends the next 5 diel cycles listening to them sing the praises of the hero who struck the raven. The raven, down to one KEAL means, is in no hurry to interrupt. Those 5 diel cycles happen to be exactly how long Suspended Animation takes before it can be used again. When Hilbert finally tears himself away and his detection roll finds the raven, it has only its Scout's Vision left to defend with. Hilbert wins again, the Scout's Vision is injured and its heart is tapped, and for the second time the raven would be wasted and is suspended instead. Now the raven has been hit twice, once for the Symbiont Barrage and once for the Scout's Vision, and saved both times by its player's personal effect. With every one of its KEAL means injured its Final Blows section appears, and only now can it be engaged in the Final Blow. It still cannot be wasted this turn, so Hilbert has to wait once more. The next day the suspension has passed, and Suspended Animation will not be ready again for several diel cycles. Now Hilbert presses the attack and engages in the Final Blow. Given that both cards have the Avian adaptation neither is at a disadvantage since two Avian adaptations do not interact. Additionally, neither motive has an advantage against the other: because Passion and Satisfaction do not interact, Hilbert does not receive the +10 bonus to the attack roll. However, the Myrthvither Raven's Satisfaction is in the Self preservation triad of motivation, so it may attempt a retreat before the Final Blow. Let's assume the raven's escape fails. Hilbert's Passion is in the Set preservation triad, which would nullify an attacker's first win were he the one defending a Final Blow; while he attacks, it does nothing for him. If the Final Blow is successful, then the defender normally gets wasted and moves out of play. See Discarding Cards and Deck Runout. If at any point the sum of the rolls and bonuses were tied, the battle match would end with a brawl. Let's assume the raven receives its final miracle and ties with Hilbert thereby starting a brawl. When we compare the value of Hilbert's HMPU, to the Myrthvither Raven's ZrrD. we see that Hilbert triumphs with a capital H over a capital Z. The battle is won, now Hilbert can return to his kingly diggs and reap the spoils of his victory! (or the game will continue on, just don't tell him that!)

title: Terrain Features
text: These cards modify territory either to benefit or hinder souls in the area. Some may be placed at random anywhere on the board, while others may offer controlled placement. These may target your opponent's territory claims, your territory claims, unclaimed territories, or any territory regardless of status. Only one terrain feature can be in play on a territory at a time. Unless otherwise specified, a new terrain feature played in a territory will replace the terrain feature card currently in play on the territory. Some of these cards must be revealed because their effects are instant and continuous. Unless stated otherwise, most terrain features are revealed at the discretion of the claim owner. If a territory is claimed with an unrevealed terrain feature, it becomes revealed to the new owner. These cannot be moved by a soul.

title: Random Territory Selection
text: Some cards apply an effect to a territory via a method of random selection. In order to properly select this territory, roll a D20 (or a D12 if you own any). If the number rolled is within the highest number on the board, then apply the effect to that territory. Otherwise, re-roll until the roll is less than or equal to the highest territory number. Alternatively, a random number generator is a good fit here. There are a bunch of free ones that you can use if you prefer

title: Trap Cards
text: Lay these in territories to activate as entities move between and through territories. These require a reasonable soul to lay them unless stated otherwise on the card. Upon moving a soul into a territory with frenemy unrevealed cards, traps must first be rolled against to see if any are activated. If the trap is activated via the conditions listed in the trap card's description, then apply its effects against the enemy attacker on top of the card stack: the consequences on the card are now in gameplay instead of dormant. If the trap is not sprung, check the roll to determine if the trap is detected. If detected, remove from play; otherwise, the trap will attempt to activate as the enemies move through the territory where it is placed. Most traps activate on a D20 roll, which is why players must always roll when entering a territory with opposing unrevealed cards. The standard numbers sit at the two ends of the die. On the low end, a 1, 2, 3, or 4 activates the trap: standard activation. On the high end, a 17, 18, 19, or 20 detects it: standard detection. The middle is dead space, where nothing happens. A card that says "Std." means these numbers. Some cards may have the ability to change these numbers, so be careful! Once laid, these cards can be moved by a soul unless otherwise stated. They remain unrevealed during movement.

title: Sabotage Cards
text: Play these cards under the cover of night and mess with your opponent's next turn. Sabotage card effects can target a wide variety of play aspects, from temporarily disabling mechanical souls to blowing up terrain features. Sabotage cards can only be played once a night. Their effects are usually applied to the next day roll; however, cards can change this if specified. Unlike most other cards in Kipukas, the effects of sabotage cards tend to be fixable under specific conditions or after a certain number of turns. Also, sabotage cards have a higher likelihood of success when compared to traps. Unlike traps; however, sabotage cards have consequences for the player who attempted the sabotage if they fail. This can be anything from jailing souls for a number of turns to wasting the soul who attempted to plant the explosive. As such, these cards have three aspects important to game play: Success Criteria, Successful Sabotage Result, and Failure Consequence. Typically, sabotage cards will state rolling a D20 against two D6 as the activation criteria.

title: Item Cards
text: These cards are used in crafting. Crafting provides potions, equipment, and other boosters. A single item will have far less power (or no power) than a crafted item. The more items used in a craft, the more powerful the final crafted item will be. Unless otherwise stated, items can be moved unrevealed by souls. Generally, if an effect or attack with an equipped item fails, you may try that effect or attack again during the next diel cycle. If a crafted item emulates another card type (i.e. trap card, soul card, etc.) please review the respective section on how to play the recipe. Items and crafted items are generally not destroyed, but rather dropped when a soul equipped with them is wasted. If a territory is under contention when this happens, each player selects a soul in the territory to grab for the item, and a brawl for it ensues: the soul with the higher brawl sequence grabs the item and equips it immediately after the brawl. No damage comes of it. If only one player has a suitable soul(s), the opponent can only defend the dropped item, not equip it: a player may always grab to keep the item from the other, and an item won that way stays dropped. If neither player has a suitable soul in the territory, the dropped item is ignored until a suitable soul moves into the conflict. Dropped items more or less belong to the territory until a soul picks them up. Hidden items stay hidden even after your opponent takes the territory.

title: Crafting
text: Crafting occurs at night, when a player combines two to three item cards according to a recipe. Once an item is crafted, keep the cards together to represent that item. In the future, we plan on letting you submit the recipe to Kipukas, then purchase a single card representation of the crafted item.   Crafted items may enhance cards from other categories or produce cards from other categories. Once applied to a card, an enhancement can be moved or removed, unless otherwise specified. Crafting character cards is the only way to have more than a single copy of a character in your deck, but you can only have one natural character card and one crafted character card. There will be no exceptions to this rule. Once an item is crafted, it either needs to be used according to the recipe's description or dropped in a controlled territory. To use dropped or hidden items in a craft, you simply pull the item from the uncontended territory and craft as normal. If a territory is taken which contains unrevealed dropped items, the items must be revealed. Control of the revealed cards, while in play, is given to the new claim holder. The claim holder must then decide to use, ignore (leave dropped), or discard the items to the card owner's discard. Hidden items (from card effects) played under the mat remain hidden from the new owner.

title: Equip Items to Souls
text: Items are often able to equip to a soul to increase some aspect of the card's abilities. Items may be equipped or unequipped any time a soul is capable of normal movement during the day, or as a part of the crafting night action. Equipped items may transfer between souls if they occupy the same territory/movement stand. An unequipped item (crafted or not) is dropped in the territory where it was unequipped. There is no limit to the number of dropped items in a territory. If a crafted item is dropped, the item remains in its crafted state and the cards remain together in a stack. A reasonable soul under the control of either player may pick up and equip these items provided they are in the same territory on an uncontested stand. When crafted or uncrafted items are equipped to a soul, move all cards together as a stack.

title: Recipes
text: During our founders period, we have released all recipe combinations that are possible to make with the founder's deck items, and any player may use any of them. To look one up, open the menu in the toolbar on kipukas.cards and choose View Item Recipes. Tick the item cards you want to combine: tick one to see what that item does alone, or two or three to see what they craft. The recipe's name and effect appear with pictures of the items it takes. Untick an item to try another combination. When a recipe is crafted, either player can check it there. See Using the Binder in the About Kipukas articles page in the binder for a screenshot and details.These recipes will always be accepted at competitions as open use, and the online lookup will always reside on the kipukas binder. As the game matures, we intend recipes to be discovered and kept for reference rather than published. This is the intended shape, not how recipes work today. We plan on making recipes into recipe cards, given out with orders (see Building Decks), for players to keep in their own recipe deck. You would present the recipe from your recipe deck to the other player to prove you can play the item combo. In competition, recipes could also be guessed and confirmed by event refs or competitors. If confirmed, you could use the recipe in the match. Only one recipe could be used in this fashion, and a wrong guess would immediately discard the items involved in the guess. We also plan on making the founder's deck recipes into recipe cards, and they will stay open use.

title: Personal Effect Cards
text: These cards are played at the beginning of the game and cannot be changed. They add an ability for the player to use throughout the game. If no player effect card is owned or the player prefers, then they can use the default effect as follows:   Place any card from the deck in front of the player. Play it in 5 diel cycles. A personal effect is used on your own turn: as your option at step 4 of Day Actions, in place of placing a card or moving a soul, or as one of your Night Actions. An effect that sets a time of its own, like the default's five diel cycles, keeps it.

title: Play Effect Examples
text:
Add to your control of a species, as a card effect towards taming it
Immediate crafting of recipes that would otherwise require a special soul to be in play
Decreased frenemy effects
Search your deck and draw any card of a given type, either at the start of the game or after so many diel cycles

title: Stealing Cards
text: We don't condone stealing another player's card out of game. However, if you would consider such a thing, I doubt you care what we think. Despite this, we are more than happy to encourage stealing in game! Cards will tell you to steal either from your opponent's hand, deck or either. You might be able to steal the cards revealed or unrevealed, depending on the instruction of the card. Either way, you begin by declaring whether you will steal from your opponent's hand or deck. Then your opponent will fan out the cards you have chosen, either facing them (unrevealed) or you (revealed). Then you pick the card that you fancy and place it in your hand. If the card allows for stealing revealed, you CANNOT scan the opponent's cards to make your decision in competitive play. For friendly play, handle that as you like. Most IMPORTANT, you CANNOT gain more than 3 cards in your hand from stealing. This is completely forbidden in Kipukas. If your stealing move would leave you with more than 3 cards in your hand it is canceled and, in competition, the card that initiated the steal is discarded. It should go without saying that stolen cards return to their original owners at the end of the game. The other options are gambling or actual thievery, in either case you should consult your local laws on the legality of your behavior.

title: Discarding Cards and Deck Runout
text:
Once a card becomes wasted, it is discarded into a pile and cannot be played again. However, some card effects target the cards in either player's discard enabling their reemergence. If you run out of cards before the end of the game, don't worry, you have not lost yet. You may continue using the cards you have in play on the kipuka. If both players run out of cards, either may still manage to take all the remaining territory even without cards in hand. Here they would win under standard conditions. Otherwise, play until no characters or species (including rogue species) are left on the kipuka. At this point, the players stop the battle under a forced peace and hold convention. Here they discuss how to proceed 
Keep the peace: Allow the player with more territories to win. If an equal number of territories is possessed, the game is a tie. (Good for a shorter game)
Call the reserves: Both players choose whether to reuse the deck they just fought with or change to another deck. If changing decks, the second deck must be pre-built, conformant and ready to play. The player who had the last soul on the kipuka states whether they will keep or use a new deck first.
 It is worth while to note that if both parties are in total agreement to keep the peace this is fully acceptable at competitions. If an agreement can't be reached within a few minutes, just rage-quit, because the other person must be pretty insufferable. Why were you playing a game with them in the first place?

title: No Summoning Sickness
text: Many games have a mechanic, often called summoning sickness, where the card that you just played can't attack in the same turn it was played. Kipukas does not, as it is in direct conflict with unrevealed cards. If a player chooses to play a soul card revealed, it is free to move and attack in the same turn it was placed. If a player chooses to play it unrevealed, it waits by that player's own choosing: it does not move or fight until it is revealed. See Unrevealed Souls in a Fight for what happens when a fight reaches it.

title: Building Decks
text: Decks are built gradually in Kipukas. To keep barriers to entry as low as possible we offer a starter kit that includes a starter map (changes by season), a starter deck or two of your choice (at first only the founder's deck is available, but more adaptation-specific starter decks will be produced), and two sets of tokens. Growing your deck after you purchase a starter kit (or if you are ambitious, before ever purchasing one) involves purchasing other starter decks separately, purchasing individual cards from kipukas.com, purchasing and waiting out the incubation period for incubation cards, or trading with people that you trust. Kipukas cards are valuable pieces of fine art, as such we take their trade and resell seriously. After launch, we intend to broker any sale or trade you request through Kipukas. This is the intended shape, not a service we offer yet. A brokered trade would involve both parties sending their cards to Kipukas. Each card in the trade would be authenticated using our 7 factor authentication process. If all cards involved in the trade are presumed authentic, we would complete the trade and send the cards to their new owners. If any cards are found to be inauthentic, the trade would be canceled, the authentic cards would be returned to their owners and the inauthentic cards would be retained by Kipukas. This process would protect your information, as neither party gets to know the other’s address, while protecting you from counterfeit cards. We also intend to put cards that you want to trade, sell, or auction on our website and inform you of offers as they are made, and to offer Kipukas Trade Deals, an exceptional trade from time to time (more often as the customer base builds).As for recipes, all of the founder's deck recipes are on the binder today (see Recipes). Once recipe cards are produced, we intend to give them out with orders: one recipe with the purchase of three cards, or three recipes with the purchase of one starter pack. You would be able to request a certain recipe in the order notes, and it would replace one of the random recipes you would have received. Recipes would then also act as information that players can trade.

title: Incubation Cards
text: These cards can be purchased, traded, won or given away just as all the other card types; however, these cannot be played. Instead, they represent an incubation time which, when complete, allows them to be traded for a soul. In time, a soul you came to own this way may come with loyalty already earned. See Affinity. The longer the incubation period, the rarer the card Kipukas will send to you. The prices of these cards are lower than the equivalent character or species available for purchase. Also, incubation cards allow access to the rarest card categories, normally reserved for competition winners and special event giveaways, if you are willing to wait out a long incubation period. The number of these cards is fixed for each category, so when they sell out, you will have to wait until one of the incubation cycles completes in order to incubate a soul of your own. For the unparalleled and winners circle rarity cards, you will be allowed to request a core adaptation. If you wish, you may also submit an artist’s rendition of the card with a backstory, then request that the card be incubated. It is not a guarantee that it will be produced; however, it may be considered.

title: Maps (The Kipukas)
text: Maps are 3D representations of territory and control. Each map hosts stands that represent traveling time and 8 to 12 territories that represent control. Each territory can host a max of 3 souls per player. In each territory there are stands for soul tokens and stands for base camp or capital tokens. Soul tokens represent the position of a revealed soul, while square base camps and capitals act as points of entry for new souls, a place for revealed or unrevealed souls to stay, and represent control of a territory. A capital is a base camp that is protected from assault until last: your opponent will not be able to take your capital until they take all other territories on the board. Card effects can also target a capital specifically. Otherwise, every rule that applies to base camps applies to capitals. See Capitals and Base Camps for all of their details in one place. Territories also represent opportunities or dangers for souls which typically dwell in or avoid the geography. See Habitat and Maps (The Kipukas): Geography. For competition purposes, only Kipukas produced boards are allowed. We do encourage adding adornments and personal flair to show off!

title: Movement
text: Each territory contains stands for placing base camp tokens and soul tokens. When a card enters the map it starts at one of the player controlled base camps or their capital, either unrevealed or revealed, dependent on the player's choice. A soul played revealed is free to move in the same day it was played. See No Summoning Sickness. As it becomes strategically advantageous, each player should choose to move their souls in play. This can be done by following the lower lines which connect between the circular movement stands and the square territory stands. Every territory hosts a max of 3 souls (per player), and each soul has a finite number of stands which it can traverse. When a soul moves, the card is placed on the mat slot with the same number as the territory moved into. In order to move, you must reveal the soul unless the card says otherwise. If an enemy is on the same stand that you moved to, you must engage an attack. Also, you cannot move past an enemy waiting on a movement stand unless a card effect permits doing so. See Attack, Defense, Retreat, and Healing; otherwise, read claiming territories below if you just moved on to a territory stand.   If a revealed soul is in a base camp, then no soul token is used. If the soul is currently on a movement stand, a soul token is used to represent this. If more than one soul is on the same movement stand, stack the individual tokens to represent the group. If you have two souls in the same territory on different movement stands, flip a soul token over and declare which soul is represented by that token. If your soul moves back into a base camp, then keep the card revealed, but remove its soul token from the board. With the exception of being totally destroyed, capitals cannot be taken until all other territories on the board are taken. However, any soul that needs to move through the opposing player's capital may do so without entering contention. It can land there on one day and needs to move out the next day. If it does not, it is the capital owner's option to take the loitering soul prisoner. See Character and Species (Souls): Imprisoned Souls. For a capital that a card removes, moves or hands over, see Capitals and Base Camps.

title: Transit Territories
text: If a territory only contains movement stands it is a transit territory. This occurs due to the difficulties required building within the territory, figuratively speaking. A good example is a territory filled with water. See Maps (The Kipukas): Geography for more information about water movement. These locations are clearly labeled on the mat as 'transit territory', so cards moved within should be placed accordingly.

title: Claiming Territories
text: In order to win the game, you must first claim territories. To claim territories, you must move at least one soul into the base camp of the territory you wish to claim. If it is empty, congrats, you have a new base camp! Place a base camp token on the terrain stand, then continue your turn. Otherwise, if the territory has a claim on it, you must oust your opponent by defeating their souls in its base camp before you can replace their claim with your own. See Contention next. There is no limit to the number of territories that can be claimed in a single day. If you think you can take all territories, including the opposing player's capital, in a single day, go for the win! See also Capitals and Base Camps.

title: Contention
text:
When souls controlled by opposing players occupy the same stand, the territory is contested. Entering your opponent's territory is a separate matter: whenever a soul moves into a territory your opponent controls, players must perform the card activation sequence, whether or not any stand is shared. See Card Activation. Card effects often activate when you enter frenemy territory, and are triggered by a D20 roll. So, always roll when entering opposing territory with unrevealed cards. You will need to contend with their traps and terrain features before attacking revealed souls.   In order to claim the territory, you must take the base camp by moving a soul onto the territory stand and alleviate contention on that stand. The base camp is the source of control for its territory: once you take it, the territory is yours, along with its terrain features and dropped items (see below), even if your opponent still has revealed souls elsewhere in the territory. Those souls are now enemies in your territory. If your opponent has multiple enemies on a stand, you can attack one or all (one at a time) of the enemies on the stand. If you decide to stop your attack or if you lose an attack, your opponent will either choose to counterattack, retreat or reinforce. If their counterattack stops before all your souls are defeated, on the following day, you have the option to continue the fight or retreat. Contention in the territory is relieved when stands only contain souls you control or souls your opponent controls, never both on the same stand. You can also reinforce the conflict. See Attack, Defense, Retreat, and Healing.   If you are not successful in taking the territory, your opponent is not obligated to reveal entities, traps, or terrain features unused in its defense. Once your opponent has exhausted all of their defense options for the base camp, and you move a soul into it, you should replace their base camp token with your base camp token. Losing a base camp results in the following change of control: 
Terrain features and dropped items are revealed if unrevealed and, while they are in play, are now controlled by the new occupier.
Souls left in the base camp are revealed if unrevealed and are imprisoned by the new occupier. See Unrevealed Souls in a Fight.
Traps are left unrevealed and stay in the control of the player who lost the base camp: they still roll activation/detection for that player. A trap detected before the base camp was taken is not among them: like any detected trap, it was removed from play when it was detected. However, if a trap left behind is detected after the base camp has changed hands, the new occupier can take control of it instead of removing it from play. See Trap Cards.
 Unrevealed Souls in a Fight# An unrevealed soul cannot engage in combat: it does not attack, and it cannot be targeted directly while it stays unrevealed. It is still there to be revealed in defense. If your opponent presses an attack past your revealed souls, or there are only unrevealed souls on the stand, the fight has reached them and the choice is yours: 
Reveal one or more of them to be engaged. If the souls you revealed win and relieve the contention, the rest may stay unrevealed.
Keep them unrevealed, and the base camp is taken. Those souls are then revealed to your opponent, along with any unrevealed terrain features, and become prisoners of the base camp. You have given up the territory for the chance to use them later. See Imprisoned Souls.
 All of this goes for a capital as it does for a base camp.

title: Capitals and Base Camps
text:
Everything about the two tokens of control, gathered in one place. Each point is told in full in the section it names. What they are 
A base camp or capital token on a territory stand represents control of that territory. The base camp is the source of control: whoever holds it holds the territory, with its terrain features and dropped items. See Contention.
They are the points of entry for new souls, and a place for revealed or unrevealed souls to stay. A revealed soul in a base camp uses no soul token. See Movement.
They are shelter: a card within a capital or base camp takes no damage from a storm. See Storm Actions.
They hold a territory's prisoners: 3 at most, on top of the 3 souls per player the territory supports. See Imprisoned Souls.
A capital is a base camp that is protected from assault until last. Card effects can also target a capital specifically. Otherwise, every rule that applies to base camps applies to capitals. See Maps.
 Placing and claiming them 
Each player places their capital during Game Setup, then claims with base camps until both players have 3 territories.
From then on, you claim a territory by moving a soul onto its territory stand: at once if it is empty, or by defeating your opponent's souls in the base camp first. See Claiming Territories.
Souls of the Digital Cloud habitat are unable to take or hold base camps or capitals. See Habitat Effects.
 Losing them 
Your opponent cannot take your capital until they have taken all other territories on the board. A soul may still pass through an opposing capital without entering contention: it can land there on one day and needs to move out the next, or the capital's owner may take it prisoner. See Movement.
Losing a base camp hands its territory over. Terrain features and dropped items go to the new occupier, souls left in the base camp are imprisoned, and traps stay with the player who lost it. See Contention and Unrevealed Souls in a Fight.
Prisoners are liberated when the base camp or capital that holds them is taken, unless the effect that imprisoned them lists other conditions. See Imprisoned Souls.
If a rogue defeats all soul cards in a territory's base camp, the claim token is removed. See Rogue Species.
Once one player claims all base camps and capitals, they win the game. See Winning the game.
 When a card removes, moves or hands over a capital 
Removed (as Meteor Shower does): the capital is truly removed from the game. The player does not lose the game, but can only work with base camps unless a card restores a capital.
Moved (as Timebattle does): the old capital is replaced by a base camp of its current owner, unless stated otherwise, and in the targeted territory the base camp is replaced by the capital token of the player who was the target of the move.
Handed over (as What Do You See in the Breach does): the capital is destroyed and replaced with the victor's base camp. Like the removed case, the player who lost the capital does not lose, but has to deal with an ordinary base camp in its place.

title: Geography
text: Each territory has a geography that corresponds to the map's topography. This geography offers habitat effects for the soul cards in the territory. See Habitat. In addition to the boat(s) marking the water habitats, Kipukas maps use docks to represent the points that souls can embark onto boats. Boats are crafted, and a finished boat is played from the hand at a dock. Boats can ferry a specified number of souls a given distance over a day. Once launched they can make land and be embarked from the last spot they landed. Either player may use a boat landed in an uncontended spot. Cards may attempt to swim by rolling 2 D6. If you roll 2 + 2 (a 2 on each die; a 1 and a 3 will not do) the card has successfully swum. It no longer needs to roll to continue swimming until it exits the water. Attempting to swim does not cost movement, but can only be attempted once per soul per day. You can attempt to swim by traversing any path leading to water.

title: Game Mats
text:
Mats connect a soul card's position with the soul token's position on the map. This makes game play more comfortable by organizing the game space. Kipukas will have a set of mats, but will encourage community development and artist support with regard to producing more engaging and creative mats. Make them as personal as you wish. The only production guidelines are as follows: 
The number of territory slots must be greater than or equal to the number of territories.
Territory reference numbers must be included and visible both with and without cards.
A transit territory slot must be allocated on the mat.

title: Story Challenging Your Opponent
text:
There is a lot going on in this game. Along the way, we will make mechanics that conflict on a reasonability level. My personal favorite example is a dragon wielding a stick to boost its attack. That is all sorts of wrong. If your opponent attempts to make a move that simply makes no sense, you have the right to contest it. The following is how you do so: 
Call them out before the effect is used in game play
Pause the battle and hold convention (have a talk)
One player must concede reasonability (either for or against)
if required, enlist a tie breaking third individual to make the final call

title: This Game is Hard!
text: Yes, it is definitely a lot to learn at first. Kipukas is a game that rewards repeated play with ease. The more you can play the game, the better you will know the card mechanics of your deck, the turn structure, and the interactions between the pieces. The overall plan is to progressively create tools to aid players in keeping track of their game. Either way, we try our best to make this rules set as comprehensive and digestible as possible. When possible, we will post videos to clarify game play aspects and intent of the mechanics. In all, don't worry about capturing every aspect of this game. As I stated, there is a lot going on. Have fun with it, make house rules, and we are always open to suggestions. These rules are geared for a future with competitions where everything will be scrutinized. At this point, don't get too bogged down and just find a way to play that is fun for you and your friends.

title: Play Style Options
text: Domination:Winner controls all territory in the kipuka. (Standard play style covered in this guide) Mass conflict:Domination with more than two players, which the game can accommodate with minimal changes to the rules. Cram as many players as you want to try onto any board you want to try it with; limiting starting territories to 1 capital and 1 base camp each is our suggestion. For future tournaments, the proposal is 8 territories = 2 players max, 9-11 territories = 3 players max, 12 territories = 4 players max. At competitions expedition boards will be available for play and purchase that will accommodate many (read a lot, gross, giant boards) more players. Same rules as Domination, but more parties means a tougher fight and more decks than are available via a starter kit at the moment. Band together:Players must work together to defeat a third party (i.e., ref, celebrity player, autonomous party, etc.), The player with the largest number of territories held wins. If the third party dominates the kipuka then both players lose. King of the hill:A territory is selected either randomly or by a ref that must be claimed and held for a number of diel cycles decided by the players to meet the victory condition. Players start with only a capital in adjacent territories. Captive:Each player gives the other a soul card, which they shuffle into their deck. Once drawn, the player must play the card unrevealed. The first player to reveal and lead their soul back to their capital wins Highest body count:Territory claims do not matter. Capitals cannot be taken. The game ends when either player runs out of cards. The victor is the player that managed to defeat the most soul cards. A number of soul cards and total card limit should be agreed upon except at competition where deck building strategy is a sizable component in this style of play The ends must justify the means:The player with the most territory gained to souls lost after a fixed number of diel cycles wins. The cost is too great:This uses standard Domination rules, but in addition it imposes a soul defeat limit that if hit removes the player from the game. Coastal war:The player to control the most coastline after a fixed number of diel cycles is the victor. The hunt:After a fixed number of diel cycles, the player with the most territories plus the hunt bonus (player with most souls with a certain type defeated receives a +3 bonus) wins. Both players must have an agreed number of those types in their decks. The huntable cards must be played and cannot be discarded. Additionally, an overall deck size must be agreed upon. Find the treasure (Special at competitions):A ref secretly marks a territory on the board with an item card, the first player to claim that territory wins the match and receives the item card. Players start with only a capital in adjacent territories. Explorer (special at competition):A ref secretly marks a territory on the board with a terrain feature, the first player to claim that territory and successfully use the card against their opponent wins the match and receives the terrain feature card. Players start with only a capital in adjacent territories. Trap Springer (special at competition):A ref secretly marks a territory on the board with a trap card, the first player to set off the trap in that territory wins the match and receives the trap card. Players start with only a capital in adjacent territories. Off to the rescue (special at competition):A ref secretly marks a territory on the board with a soul card, the first player to claim that territory and usher the survivor back to their capital wins the match and receives the soul’s card. Players start with only a capital in adjacent territories Cradle Robber (special at competition):A ref secretly marks a territory on the board with an incubation card drawn from a bag, with scarcity proportional to the incubation cards in circulation. The first person to find and take the surrounding territories (thereby protecting the card) wins the match and receives the incubation card. Players start with only a capital in adjacent territories.
